newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Supreme Court to hear English-only arguments.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Supreme Court to hear English-only arguments.

text.p: The Supreme Court Wednesday hears a constitutional free-speech challenge to a controversial law that requires all Arizona state workers to speak only English on the job.

Arizona voters in 1988 barely approved an initiative barring the use of any language other than English by all state employees while performing their official duties. The measure provides penalties for violators.
The Arizona measure was the most restrictive and sweeping of the laws that have been adopted by about half of the states declaring English the official language.

The case reached the nine justices after a U.S. appeals court in California ruled that the measure violated the free-speech rights, guaranteed under the Constitution's First Amendment, of the state employees.
The Arizona law had been challenged in court in 1988 by Maria-Kelley Yniguez, an employee of the department of administration who handled medical malpractice claims against the state.

Fluent in English and Spanish, she spoke Spanish to some claimants. But she stopped speaking Spanish at work after the law had been approved and filed a lawsuit claiming the measure violated her constitutional rights.

Appealing to the Supreme Court in defending the law was a group called Arizonans for Official English, which argued that a state may require its employees to use a certain language. Arizona earlier in the legal battle decided against appealing.
The high court may end up deciding the case on technical grounds rather than reaching the constitutional issue.
The Supreme Court will consider whether the English-only group, instead of the state, can proceed with the appeal and if there is an actual case or controversy involving Yniguez.

The Justice Department told the high court the case presents procedural problems because the private English-only group lacked proper legal standing to appeal in place of the state. It also said Yniguez had left her state job in 1990, ending the controversy.
The case has stirred interest in Congress, where the English-only question has become a divisive, hotly debated issue.

More than 50 Senate and House members filed a brief opposing the Arizona measure. Representative Nydia Velazquez, one of the lawmakers, denounced English-only laws as "discriminatory and undemocratic."
But a group of 21 House Republicans, including a number of conservatives, expressed strong support for the Arizona law.
